246.title: The other cheek (Matthew 5:38–42)
246.hook: no revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, go the second mile
246.howItsDone: The peace churches, such as Mennonites, Quakers and the Church of the Brethren, read this as a call to nonviolence; many other Christians apply it to personal insult and revenge, and practice it through forgiveness and generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, let your yes be yes, and your line was yes means yes. Did you drop the boosters and just say what you meant? Day two hundred forty-six.

Somebody shoves you in line. Somebody posts something cruel about you. Somebody takes your parking space, then smirks. Everything in you wants to even the score. And maybe a little more than even, just so they learn. The next lines of the sermon are hard ones. Turn the other cheek. Go the extra mile. People who've never opened a Bible use them. But to hear them properly, you have to start with the old rule he's quoting.
screen: `EVEN THE SCORE.` → `TURN THE OTHER CHEEK.` → `START WITH THE OLD RULE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth." That's from the law of Moses. It's often read as a limit on revenge rather than a command to take it: one eye for one eye, not a whole family for an eye. And in Jewish tradition, the rabbis read it as fair compensation paid in court, not literal injury. Jesus goes further still. "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Then three pictures. If someone sues you for your coat, give him your cloak too. And, in the King James Bible: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." That word compel had a specific use: scholars say it meant soldiers and officials pressing locals into service, like carrying gear. It's the same Greek word Mark uses when the soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross. So picture it: a soldier of the occupying army orders you to haul his pack. The order is one mile. Jesus says: go two. Scholars read these sayings in different ways. Some, like the scholar Walter Wink, argue that a slap on the right cheek was a backhanded insult, and turning the other cheek was a nonviolent way of standing your ground with dignity. Others read it more simply as refusing to retaliate at all. Churches differ, too: the peace churches say it rules out violence entirely; many other Christians say it governs personal revenge, not every use of force. What these readings share is the direction: break the cycle. Don't pay back.
screen: `AN EYE FOR AN EYE: A LIMIT.` · `TURN TO HIM THE OTHER ALSO.` · `COMPEL: A SOLDIER'S PACK.` · `BREAK THE CYCLE.` · then, large: `GO WITH HIM TWAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go one extra mile for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who asks more of you than you'd like: a demanding boss, a needy relative, a neighbor who always wants a favor. Picture the thing they usually ask for. Now picture doing that, and then a little more, freely, before they ask. Not because you have to. Because you choose to. If it would put you in danger or let someone abuse you, that's not this. If you pray, you can ask for a free heart. The bell holds the time.
The other cheek. No revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, and when you're forced to go one mile, go two.
Your line: the second mile. Today, when someone asks something of you, do what they asked, and then one small thing more, freely. Day two hundred forty-six.

fork.reveal: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." do more than you're forced to, freely.

what it means: refuse to pay back; break the cycle of revenge, and do more good than is demanded.

247.title: Love your enemies (Matthew 5:43–48)
247.hook: pray for those who persecute you; the sun rises on the evil and the good
247.howItsDone: Some churches include prayers for enemies and those who wish harm in their regular intercessions, and Christians turn to this passage when facing conflict, war or personal injury.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the other cheek, and your line was the second mile. Did you do one small thing more, freely? Day two hundred forty-seven.

Tomorrow morning the sun will come up over your street. It will come through the window of the kindest person you know. And it will come through the window of the person you like least in the world, at exactly the same time, just as warm. The rain will fall on both your yards. The sky doesn't check anyone's record first. Jesus points to that ordinary fact, and builds a hard command on it.
screen: `THE SUN ON YOUR STREET.` → `THE PERSON YOU LIKE LEAST.` → `THE SKY DOESN'T CHECK.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy. The first half is from Leviticus: love thy neighbor as thyself. The second half isn't a verse anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, and nobody knows for sure where the saying came from. The book of Proverbs, in fact, says: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." Then Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." The word for love here is agape, which Christian teachers often explain not as a warm feeling but as a choice to seek someone's good. You may never like your enemy. You can still want good for them. Why? "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." That's God's way, Jesus says: generous to everyone. If you love only those who love you, he adds, what reward is that? Even the tax collectors do the same. Then the last line of the chapter: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. The Greek word, teleios, means whole, complete, grown up. Not flawless. Complete in love, the way the sun is complete, shining on every yard. Christians have tried to live this in extreme places: forgiving the people who killed their families, praying for their jailers. Jesus himself, Luke says, prayed from the cross for those crucifying him.
screen: `LOVE THY NEIGHBOR, HATE THINE ENEMY?` · `AGAPE: CHOOSING SOMEONE'S GOOD.` · `SUN AND RAIN ON EVERYONE.` · `TELEIOS: WHOLE, COMPLETE.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for one enemy by name. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind: someone who has hurt you, opposed you, or simply wears you out. Say their name quietly. If you pray, pray for them: for their health, their family, their peace. If you don't pray, simply wish them one good thing, sincerely. You don't have to feel warm. You don't have to trust them. Just picture the sun rising on their house, too. The bell holds the time.
Love your enemies. Agape: choosing someone's good, even when they're against you, the way the sun shines on everyone.
Your line: the sun shines on all. Today, when the sun or the rain touches you, think of the person you like least, and wish them the same. Day two hundred forty-seven.

248.title: Not to be seen (Matthew 6:1–6)
248.hook: give, pray and fast in secret; your Father sees in secret
248.howItsDone: This passage is read in many churches on Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, when Christians take up quiet giving, prayer and fasting; some give anonymously and keep a private time of prayer each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love your enemies, and your line was the sun shines on all. Did you wish someone difficult a little sunlight? Day two hundred forty-eight.

Have you ever done something kind and then felt the tiny itch to post about it? A donation, a volunteer shift, a good deed. Just a small photo. Just so people know. That pull is nothing new. Now Jesus turns to three practices of his people's faith: giving to the poor, praying and fasting. He doesn't say don't do them. He assumes you will. He asks something sharper: who are you doing them for?
screen: `THE ITCH TO POST IT.` → `GIVING, PRAYING, FASTING.` → `WHO ARE YOU DOING IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Take heed, he says, that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them. Don't sound a trumpet when you give, the way the hypocrites do, to be praised. Nobody's sure anyone literally blew trumpets; it may be a vivid picture, like our blowing your own horn. Then, in the King James Bible: "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Give so quietly that even you half forget it. The word hypocrite is worth opening. In Greek, hupokrites meant a stage actor, someone who performed behind a mask. Jesus's point isn't about any one group. It's about anyone, in any faith or none, who performs goodness for an audience. And he says of them, three times: they have their reward. Scholars point out that the Greek verb turns up on ancient receipts: paid in full. They wanted applause, they got it, and that's the whole payment. Then prayer: don't pray on street corners to be seen. Instead, in the King James Bible: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which is in secret shall reward thee openly." Closet here means an inner room, maybe a storeroom, the one room in a small house with a door. It doesn't mean praying together is wrong; Luke says Jesus went to the synagogue on the sabbath, as his custom was, and he taught his friends a prayer that begins our Father. It's about the audience. The same goes for fasting: wash your face, look normal, and let it be between you and God. Thy Father which is in secret, he says, sees it. On his telling, the quiet good isn't wasted.
screen: `NO TRUMPETS.` · `HUPOKRITES: AN ACTOR IN A MASK.` · `THEY HAVE THEIR REWARD: PAID IN FULL.` · `SHUT THY DOOR.` · then, large: `THY FATHER WHICH IS IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray behind a closed door. If you can, go into a room right now and shut the door. A bedroom, a bathroom, a parked car, anywhere with no audience. Sit down. Notice what it's like to be unseen. Nobody to impress. Nothing to perform. If you pray, you can speak to God here as simply as you'd speak to someone you trust. If you don't, just rest in the quiet, and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
Not to be seen. Give, pray and fast without an audience, because the Father sees in secret.
Your line: the father sees in secret. Today, do one good thing and tell no one. Not now, not later. Let it stay unseen. Day two hundred forty-eight.

249.title: Not many words (Matthew 6:7–8)
249.hook: your Father knows what you need before you ask
249.howItsDone: Christians pray both in set words and in their own words: Catholics and Orthodox often use repeated prayers like the rosary and the Jesus Prayer, and many Protestants favor short spontaneous prayers; across the churches, prayer is often described as turning toward God rather than informing him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not to be seen, and your line was the father sees in secret. Did you do one good thing and tell no one? Day two hundred forty-nine.

Some people feel they can't pray because they don't know the right words. They've heard others pray beautifully, long flowing sentences, and they freeze. Others pray the way we write emails to someone important: carefully, at length, explaining everything, just in case. Both are really asking the same question: how much do I have to say to be heard? Right after telling his listeners to shut the door and pray in secret, Jesus answers that question.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `PRAYING LIKE A LONG EMAIL.` → `HOW MUCH DO I HAVE TO SAY?`

segments.voice: When you pray, he says, don't babble on, thinking you'll be heard because of your many words. The Greek verb here is battalogeo. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Nobody knows exactly where it comes from. Some scholars think it's a sound word, like our blah-blah-blah: batta-batta. Heaping up syllables. Then the reason, in the King James Bible: "your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." That changes what prayer is for. You're not informing God. You're not filing a report. He already knows, Jesus says. So why pray at all? Christians have long asked that, and one common answer is: because prayer isn't mainly for passing on information. It's for being with someone. A friend who sits beside you in a hospital waiting room isn't there to pass on news. They're there to be with you. Now, a fair question: what about repeating prayers? Christians read this verse in different ways. Catholics pray the rosary, Orthodox Christians repeat the Jesus Prayer, and they say the warning is against empty words, not repeated ones. After all, in Gethsemane, Mark says Jesus "went away, and prayed, and spake the same words." Some Protestant Christians hear the verse as a caution against praying by rote, and favor praying in their own words. Both agree on the heart: it's not the number of words that reaches God. The very next thing Jesus does is teach a short prayer. Tomorrow, we'll look at it again.
screen: `BATTALOGEO: BLAH-BLAH-BLAH.` · `HE KNOWETH BEFORE YE ASK.` · `PRAYER: TURNING TOWARD SOMEONE.` · `EMPTY WORDS, NOT REPEATED ONES.` · then, large: `YOUR FATHER KNOWETH WHAT THINGS YE HAVE NEED OF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray in ten words or fewer. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing that's weighing on you most today. Now shrink it down. Not a paragraph. Ten words or fewer. Help my mother. I'm afraid about tomorrow. Thank you for this morning. If you pray, say those few words to God, once, and then just sit, trusting that he already knows the rest. If you don't pray, simply name it, and let the silence hold it. The bell holds the time.
Not many words. Don't babble on to be heard; your Father knows what you need before you ask.
Your line: he already knows. Today, when a worry comes, put it in ten words or fewer, say it once, and let it go. Day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: The prayer again (Matthew 6:9–15)
250.hook: the Lord's Prayer, set here in the middle of the sermon
250.howItsDone: Christians of every church pray the Lord's Prayer, in worship and at home; many pray it daily, and in most churches the congregation says it together, aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not many words, and your line was he already knows. Did you put one worry into ten words or fewer? Day two hundred fifty.

Way back at the start of this path, in the first weeks, we walked through the Lord's Prayer one line at a time. Our Father. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. You might know it by heart now. But a prayer you know by heart can slip past you, like the words of a song you've sung a thousand times. So today we meet it again, in a new place: not on its own, but set right in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount. Where it sits changes how it sounds.
screen: `BACK AT THE START OF THE PATH.` → `A PRAYER KNOWN BY HEART.` → `IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SERMON.`

segments.voice: Jesus has just said: don't pray to be seen, and don't babble. Then, in the King James Bible: "After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." After this manner: a pattern as well as a script. Short, plain, private enough to say behind a closed door, and yet it says our, not my. Many scholars notice that it sits near the very center of the sermon, as if the whole teaching turns around it. Everything before it, the Beatitudes, reconciling, loving enemies, is what it looks like when thy will be done on earth. For centuries, Western Christians prayed it in Latin, and its first two words, Pater noster, our Father, became a word of their own. Medieval prayer beads were called paternosters. A street near Saint Paul's Cathedral in London is still called Paternoster Row. There's even a kind of open elevator, a chain of little rooms that never stops moving, called a paternoster, because it goes round and round like beads in praying hands. At the end, Matthew adds a line about forgiveness: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." It's the only line of the prayer Jesus explains. And the ending many people know, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory? It's in the King James Bible, but not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew. It was likely added early for worship. Protestants usually pray it with the prayer; at Mass, Catholics say it a little later, after the priest's prayer.
screen: `AFTER THIS MANNER: A PATTERN.` · `AT THE CENTER OF THE SERMON.` · `PATER NOSTER: BEADS, A ROW, AN ELEVATOR.` · `FORGIVE, AND FOR THINE IS THE KINGDOM.` · then, large: `THY WILL BE DONE IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a line per breath. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, pray the Lord's Prayer very slowly: one line on each breath. Our Father, which art in heaven. Breathe. Hallowed be thy name. Breathe. Let each line land before you move on. If a line catches, stay there. If you don't pray, simply listen to the lines in your mind as words people have said for two thousand years, and notice which one stays with you. The bell holds the time.
Paternoster. Latin for our Father: the first words of the Lord's Prayer, which became a name for prayer beads, a London street and an elevator.
Your line: thy will be done. Today, at the moment you most want your own way, say those four words, silently, and see what changes. Day two hundred fifty.

251.title: Moths and rust (Matthew 6:19–21)
251.hook: where your treasure is, there your heart will be
251.howItsDone: Some Christians give a regular share of their income to church and to the poor, often following the biblical tithe, and think of generosity as laying up treasure in heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer again, paternoster, and your line was thy will be done. When did you say it, and what changed? Day two hundred fifty-one.

Open a drawer you haven't opened in years. The sweater you loved has holes in it. The gadget that cost a week's pay won't turn on. The box of things you couldn't live without, you'd forgotten you had. Plenty of homes have a drawer like that. It's a little funny, and a little sobering. Things we once treasured, quietly falling apart while we weren't looking. Jesus's listeners had drawers like that too. And he starts a new part of the sermon right there.
screen: `A DRAWER YOU HAVEN'T OPENED.` → `HOLES IN THE SWEATER.` → `THINGS WE ONCE TREASURED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal." In his world, wealth could mean fine clothing, which moths could eat, and stored goods and metal, which could spoil and corrode. The Greek word translated rust literally means eating: anything that eats away, corrosion or vermin. And thieves break through: in Greek, dig through. The picture is of a burglar who doesn't pick a lock; he digs through the wall. Nothing on earth is completely safe. Then comes the line that turns it all around: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Notice the order. We usually assume the heart leads and the money follows: I care about this, so I spend on it. Jesus says it also works the other way. Put your treasure somewhere, and your heart goes after it. That's why this is hopeful. If you want to care more about something, you can start by giving to it. So what are treasures in heaven? Christians describe them as what can't be eaten by moths: love given, mercy shown, the poor helped, time spent on what lasts. Read this way, Jesus isn't saying money doesn't matter. Money is more like a compass: it shows where your heart is heading. Your bank statement, you could say, is a kind of spiritual diary.
screen: `MOTH, RUST, THIEVES.` · `RUST: WHATEVER EATS AWAY.` · `BREAK THROUGH: DIG THROUGH THE WALL.` · `THE HEART FOLLOWS THE TREASURE.` · then, large: `THERE WILL YOUR HEART BE ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at where your money went this week. Settle, and breathe. Picture your spending since last week, or open it up if you can. Don't judge yourself. Just read it like a diary. What does it say you care about? Where is your heart being pulled? Notice one thing that surprises you. Then notice one thing that lasts: a gift, a meal shared, a kindness. If you pray, you can offer both to God. The bell holds the time.
Moths and rust. Whatever eats away earthly treasure, and the line that follows: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Your line: where your treasure is. Today, put a little treasure, money or time, into something you want your heart to follow. Day two hundred fifty-one.

screen: `DAY 251 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LAMP OF THE BODY.`

252.title: The lamp of the body (Matthew 6:22–24)
252.hook: the eye is the lamp; you can't serve God and mammon
252.howItsDone: Christians often speak of stewardship, holding money as something entrusted by God, and some practice regular giving, simple living or fasting from spending as ways to keep money a servant rather than a master.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moths and rust, and your line was where your treasure is. Where did you put a little treasure, and did your heart follow? Day two hundred fifty-two, the end of the week.

Try working for two bosses at once. One wants the report by noon; the other wants you at a meeting at noon. One says cut costs; the other says spend. Sooner or later, you pick one, and the other one notices. Two jobs, or two households with different rules, work the same way. Jesus has just said the heart follows the treasure. Now he pushes it further, with two pictures: a lamp, and a servant with two masters.
screen: `TWO BOSSES AT ONCE.` → `SOONER OR LATER, YOU PICK ONE.` → `A LAMP, AND TWO MASTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the lamp. In the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light." Single here translates a Greek word that can mean simple, undivided, and also generous. In Jewish idiom, a good eye meant a generous person, and an evil eye meant a stingy one. Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he gives his bread to the poor. So a single eye looks at the world openly and generously, and the whole person fills with light. A grasping eye darkens everything. Then the second picture, in the King James Bible: "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Serve here means serve as a slave. Not a part-time job. A slave can't belong fully to two owners. And mammon? It's an Aramaic word for wealth or property, the stuff you own and rely on. Some scholars think it comes from a root meaning that in which you trust, though nobody is sure. It wasn't the name of a god; medieval writers later turned Mammon into a demon, and the poet Milton put him in Paradise Lost. But Jesus uses it almost like a person, a rival master, because that's how money can act: it makes demands, it promises safety, it asks for your time and your worry. Look back at this week: the other cheek, love for enemies, giving in secret, few words, our Father, moths and rust, and now one master. Each asks: who, finally, do you belong to?
screen: `THE EYE IS THE LAMP.` · `SINGLE: UNDIVIDED, GENEROUS.` · `NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.` · `MAMMON: WEALTH YOU TRUST.` · then, large: `YE CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you look at most. Settle, and breathe. Think back over today. What did your eyes keep going to? Price tags, other people's things, your balance, a face you love? No verdict. Just notice where your eye kept landing. Then picture your eye as a lamp: what would it look like to see today with a generous eye? If you pray, you can ask for a single eye. The bell holds the time.
Mammon. Aramaic for wealth, the things you own and trust; Jesus names it as a rival master. You can't serve both.
Your line: one master. Today, when money makes a demand on your worry, remind yourself who you belong to, and do one generous thing with a single eye. Day two hundred fifty-two.

match.prompt: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

myth: Mammon was the name of an ancient god
it's an Aramaic word for wealth; medieval writers later made it a demon.
in Jewish idiom a good eye meant a generous person
and an evil eye meant a stingy one.
serve here means serve as a slave
a slave can't belong fully to two owners.

fork.setup: you're trying to serve God and money equally, giving each a fair share of your heart. what does Jesus say?
options: no one can serve two masters.
fork.reveal: "No man can serve two masters ... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." sooner or later, you hold to one.

original.note: Greek spelling of an Aramaic word: wealth, property. Matthew 6:24.

trapdoor: what you thought: mammon is an old word for the devil.
what it means: it's wealth, what you own and rely on, pictured as a rival master.
what a scholar hears: mammon is Aramaic, perhaps from a root meaning that in which one trusts; a single eye is haplous, generous.
